stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether an expected reward reduces children's later interest in drawing. They recruited 60 preschool children who enjoyed drawing and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Children in one condition were promised a certificate for drawing and received it. Children in the other condition drew with no reward mentioned. The researchers then recorded the number of minutes that each child chose to spend drawing during free time one week later.
Researchers collected data from 250 adults. For each one, they recorded resting heart rate and self-rated anxiety. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.38.

Researchers investigated whether nausea after a new taste produces an aversion to that taste. They recruited 40 laboratory rats and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Rats in one condition drank sweetened water and were then given an injection that causes mild nausea. Rats in the other condition drank sweetened water and were then given a harmless salt-water injection. The researchers then recorded the volume in milliliters of sweetened water that each rat drank the next day.

Researchers investigated whether the presence of other people slows the reporting of an emergency. They recruited 80 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition were filling in a form in a room with four other people when smoke began to enter the room. Participants in the other condition were filling in the form alone when smoke began to enter the room. The researchers then recorded the time in seconds before each participant left the room to report the smoke.

Researchers investigated whether a smiling expression makes cartoons seem funnier. They recruited 90 university students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition held a pen between their teeth, which produces a smile. Participants in the other condition held a pen between their lips, which prevents a smile. The researchers then recorded the rating from 1 to 10 that each participant gave to a set of cartoons.

Researchers investigated whether spreading study sessions out improves long-term retention. They recruited 90 high school students and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition studied a list of 40 words in six ten-minute sessions on six different days. Participants in the other condition studied the same list in a single sixty-minute session. The researchers then recorded the number of words out of 40 that each participant recalled on a test one month later. The results are shown in the table. The difference between the two groups had a p value of 0.41.

rows.group: The group that studied in six short sessions
The group that studied in one long session

stimuli.text: Researchers investigated whether keeping a gratitude journal raises well-being. They recruited 110 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition wrote down three things they were grateful for every night for a month. Participants in the other condition wrote down three things they had done every night for a month. The researchers then recorded each participant's rating of life satisfaction on a scale from 1 to 10 at the end of the month.

Researchers collected data from 600 university students. For each one, they recorded conscientiousness score on a personality inventory and grade point average. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.35.

Researchers investigated whether the color of a drink affects the ability to identify its flavor. They recruited 70 adult volunteers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition tasted ten fruit drinks whose colors did not match their flavors. Participants in the other condition tasted the same ten drinks with matching colors. The researchers then recorded the number of flavors out of ten that each participant named correctly.

Researchers investigated whether cognitive-behavioral therapy reduces depression. They recruited 90 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition received twelve weekly sessions of cognitive-behavioral therapy. Participants in the other condition were placed on a waiting list for twelve weeks and were treated afterward. The researchers then recorded each participant's score on a standard depression questionnaire after twelve weeks.

Researchers investigated whether mindfulness meditation lowers stress. They recruited 84 office workers and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition practiced mindfulness meditation for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. Participants in the other condition listened to an audiobook for twenty minutes a day for eight weeks. The researchers then recorded the level of the stress hormone cortisol in a saliva sample from each participant.

Researchers investigated whether regular aerobic exercise improves memory in older adults. They recruited 100 adults aged 60 to 75 and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Participants in one condition walked briskly for 40 minutes three times a week for six months. Participants in the other condition did gentle stretching for the same amount of time. The researchers then recorded the number of locations that each participant correctly recalled on a spatial memory test.

Researchers collected data from 1,200 teenagers. For each one, they recorded the number of hours of social media use per day and score on a depression questionnaire. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.28.

Researchers investigated whether agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a large one. They recruited 120 homeowners and randomly assigned each one to one of two conditions. Homeowners in one condition were first asked to sign a road-safety petition and two weeks later were asked to put a large sign in their garden. Homeowners in the other condition were only asked to put the large sign in their garden. The researchers then recorded the percentage of homeowners in each group who agreed to display the sign.

Researchers collected data from 300 families. For each one, they recorded the warmth of parenting, as rated by observers and the child's self-esteem score. The correlation between the two measures was r = +0.48.

Read the summary of a hypothetical study, then answer parts A to F.

**Introduction.** Researchers investigated whether children imitate aggressive behavior that they observe. They hypothesized that the behavior of an adult model would affect aggressive behavior.

**Participants.** The sample was 72 preschool children, recruited from one city. Parents gave informed consent, each child gave assent, and the plan was approved by an institutional review board. Families could withdraw at any time.

**Method.** The children were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. Children in one condition watched a video of an adult hitting an inflatable doll. Children in the other condition watched a video of an adult playing quietly with other toys. The researchers recorded the number of times that each child hit the doll during ten minutes of free play.

**Results.** The group that watched the aggressive adult: mean number of hits = 14.2. The group that watched the quiet adult: mean number of hits = 3.1. The difference was statistically significant (p = 0.01).

Use the three hypothetical sources to answer the question: **Do rewards increase motivation?**

**Source A.** In an experiment, 60 preschool children who liked drawing were randomly assigned to draw for a promised certificate or to draw with no reward. A week later, during free play, the rewarded children chose to draw for a mean of 6.5 minutes and the unrewarded children for 13.8 minutes (p = 0.01).

**Source B.** In a study of 200 call-center workers, half were randomly assigned to receive a bonus for each sale. Over a month, the bonus group made a mean of 41 sales and the comparison group a mean of 33 (p = 0.02). When the bonus ended, the bonus group's sales fell to a mean of 30.

**Source C.** A survey of 500 university students found that students who said they studied mainly because they found their subject interesting had higher grades and reported less burnout than students who said they studied mainly for grades or money (r = +0.40 between interest and grades).

questions.stem: As well as obtaining permission from the parents, the researchers asked each child whether he or she was willing to take part. What is the child's agreement called?

options.why: Confidentiality is keeping data private.
Debriefing happens after the study.
Deception is misleading participants about the study.
Correct. Minors cannot give legal consent, so they give assent and their parents give consent.

questions.explanation: Minors cannot give legal consent, so they give assent and their parents give consent.

questions.stem: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus?

options.why: The synapse is the tiny gap between the sending neuron and the receiving neuron.
The axon is the long fiber that carries the neural impulse away from the cell body toward other cells.
Correct. The cell body is the part of the neuron that contains the nucleus and keeps the cell alive.
The axon terminals is the endings of the axon that release neurotransmitters.

questions.explanation: The cell body is the part of the neuron that contains the nucleus and keeps the cell alive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the identity status of a person who has neither explored options nor made a commitment?

options.why: Identity moratorium is the identity status of a person who is actively exploring options but has not yet made a commitment.
Identity achievement is the identity status of a person who has explored options and made a commitment.
Correct. Identity diffusion is the identity status of a person who has neither explored options nor made a commitment.
Identity foreclosure is the identity status of a person who has made a commitment without exploring options.

questions.explanation: Identity diffusion is the identity status of a person who has neither explored options nor made a commitment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the fovea?

options.text: The central point of the retina, where cones are packed most densely and vision is sharpest
options.why: Correct. This is what the fovea means.

options.text: The receptor cells that detect color and fine detail and work in bright light
options.why: That describes cones.

options.text: The transparent structure that changes shape to focus light on the retina
options.why: That describes the lens.

options.text: The point where the optic nerve leaves the eye, which has no receptor cells
options.why: That describes the blind spot.

questions.explanation: The fovea is the central point of the retina, where cones are packed most densely and vision is sharpest.

questions.stem: An expert pool player makes more of her shots when a crowd is watching than when she plays alone. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Deindividuation is the loss of self-awareness and self-restraint in group situations that provide arousal and anonymity.
Groupthink is the kind of thinking in which the desire for agreement in a group overrides a realistic evaluation of alternatives.
Correct. Social facilitation is the improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks in the presence of others.
Group polarization is the strengthening of a group's existing opinions after the members discuss them.

questions.explanation: Social facilitation is the improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks in the presence of others.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the brief sensory memory of a visual image, which lasts a few tenths of a second?

options.why: Short-term memory is the memory store that briefly holds a few items, about seven, before they are stored or forgotten.
Working memory is the active processing of information held in mind, combining new input with knowledge from long-term memory.
Correct. Iconic memory is the brief sensory memory of a visual image, which lasts a few tenths of a second.
Long-term memory is the relatively permanent and limitless store of knowledge, skills and experiences.

questions.explanation: Iconic memory is the brief sensory memory of a visual image, which lasts a few tenths of a second.

questions.stem: After two neurons fire together repeatedly, the synapse between them becomes more efficient. What is this process called?

options.why: The visuospatial sketchpad is the part of working memory that briefly holds images and spatial information.
The phonological loop is the part of working memory that briefly holds spoken and written words.
Correct. Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of the connections between neurons after repeated activation, which is the biological basis of memory.
The central executive is the part of working memory that directs attention and coordinates the other parts.

questions.explanation: Long-term potentiation is the strengthening of the connections between neurons after repeated activation, which is the biological basis of memory.

questions.stem: Damage to a network running through the brainstem leaves a patient in a coma, unable to be woken. Which structure is damaged?

options.why: The cerebellum is the structure at the back of the brainstem that coordinates balance, movement and procedural learning.
The thalamus is the brain's sensory relay station, which directs incoming signals to the cortex.
Correct. The reticular activating system is the network of neurons in the brainstem that controls arousal and alertness.
The medulla is the base of the brainstem, which controls heartbeat and breathing.

questions.explanation: The reticular activating system is the network of neurons in the brainstem that controls arousal and alertness.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes displacement?

options.text: The defense mechanism of giving a comfortable excuse in place of the real reason for a behavior
options.why: That describes rationalization.

options.text: The defense mechanism of refusing to accept a painful reality
options.why: That describes denial.

options.text: The defense mechanism of shifting an impulse from its real target to a safer one
options.why: Correct. This is what displacement means.

options.text: The defense mechanism of seeing one's own unacceptable impulses in other people
options.why: That describes projection.

questions.explanation: Displacement is the defense mechanism of shifting an impulse from its real target to a safer one.

questions.stem: Can the researchers conclude that resting heart rate causes a change in self-rated anxiety?

options.text: No, because a correlation does not show cause and effect
options.why: Correct. Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

options.text: Yes, because the correlation is not zero
options.why: Any nonzero correlation still leaves the cause unknown.

options.text: Yes, because the sample was large
options.why: A large sample does not turn a correlation into evidence of causation.

options.text: No, because correlations can only be calculated in experiments
options.why: Correlations are calculated in non-experimental studies.

questions.explanation: Without manipulating a variable and assigning subjects at random, other explanations cannot be ruled out.

questions.stem: In a drug trial, half of the patients receive no active medication so that their results can be compared with the others. This half is which of the following?

options.why: Correct. The control group is the group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment and is used for comparison.
Statistical significance is the conclusion that a result is unlikely to have occurred by chance, usually when p is below 0.05.
The experimental group is the group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.
A confounding variable is a factor other than the independent variable that differs between groups and could explain the results.

questions.explanation: The control group is the group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment and is used for comparison.

questions.stem: In a crowd of fans, people see the red-shirted fans as one group and the blue-shirted fans as another. Which Gestalt principle explains this?

options.why: Figure and ground is the Gestalt principle that we organize a scene into an object that stands out and its background.
Proximity is the Gestalt principle that we group together objects that are near each other.
Correct. Similarity is the Gestalt principle that we group together objects that look alike.
Closure is the Gestalt principle that we fill in gaps to see a complete, whole object.

questions.explanation: Similarity is the Gestalt principle that we group together objects that look alike.

questions.stem: After the election result is announced, Tom says, 'I knew all along that she would win,' although he had predicted the opposite. Which bias is this?

options.why: Correct. Hindsight bias is the tendency, after learning an outcome, to believe one would have predicted it.
Self-report bias is the inaccuracy that arises when people describe their own behavior or feelings.
Experimenter bias is the influence of a researcher's expectations on the results of a study.
Social desirability bias is the tendency of participants to answer in a way that makes them look good.

questions.explanation: Hindsight bias is the tendency, after learning an outcome, to believe one would have predicted it.

questions.stem: No matter how hard she tries, Zara cannot remember anything from before she was three. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Correct. Infantile amnesia is the inability of adults to remember events from the first few years of life.
Alzheimer's disease is a progressive brain disease that destroys memory and then other mental abilities.
Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after an injury or illness.
Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories from before an injury or illness.

questions.explanation: Infantile amnesia is the inability of adults to remember events from the first few years of life.

questions.stem: At seventy, Mr. Park is slower than he used to be at solving unfamiliar logic puzzles. Which kind of intelligence has declined?

options.why: The zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and what the learner can do with help.
Correct. Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason quickly and abstractly, which tends to decline in older adulthood.
Crystallized intelligence is the accumulated knowledge and verbal skills that tend to increase with age.
Scaffolding is the temporary support that a more skilled person gives a learner and gradually removes.

questions.explanation: Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason quickly and abstractly, which tends to decline in older adulthood.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the primacy effect?

options.text: The finding that study spread over time produces better long-term memory than study crammed together
options.why: That describes the spacing effect.

options.text: The tendency to remember the first and last items in a list better than the middle ones
options.why: That describes the serial position effect.

options.text: The tendency to remember the first items in a list well
options.why: Correct. This is what the primacy effect means.

options.text: The tendency to remember the last items in a list well
options.why: That describes the recency effect.

questions.explanation: The primacy effect is the tendency to remember the first items in a list well.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the reducing of stress by managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor?

options.why: Correct. Emotion-focused coping is the reducing of stress by managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor.
Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure, which is made more likely by chronic stress.
Problem-focused coping is the reducing of stress by changing the stressor itself or the way one deals with it.
Immune suppression is the weakening of the body's defenses against illness during long-term stress.

questions.explanation: Emotion-focused coping is the reducing of stress by managing one's emotional reaction rather than the stressor.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes group therapy?

options.text: The technique of echoing, restating and seeking clarification of what the client says
options.why: That describes active listening.

options.text: A state of heightened suggestibility that can help reduce pain and anxiety but does not reliably recover memories
options.why: That describes hypnosis.

options.text: The psychodynamic technique of analyzing dreams to uncover unconscious wishes and conflicts
options.why: That describes dream interpretation.

options.text: The therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support
options.why: Correct. This is what group therapy means.

questions.explanation: Group therapy is the therapy in which several clients meet together with a therapist and benefit from each other's support.

questions.stem: Which group served as the control group?

options.text: Neither group, because the study had no comparison condition
options.why: The second condition is the comparison.

options.text: The group given the salt-water injection
options.why: Correct. The control group is the comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested.

options.text: The group given the nausea-causing injection
options.why: This group received the treatment being tested: it is the experimental group.
Only the comparison group is the control group.

questions.explanation: The control group is the comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes transcendence?

options.text: The category of character strengths that includes gratitude, hope, humor and appreciation of beauty
options.why: Correct. This is what transcendence means.

options.text: The category of character strengths that includes bravery, honesty and perseverance
options.why: That describes courage.

options.text: The category of character strengths that includes forgiveness, humility and self-control
options.why: That describes temperance.

options.text: The category of character strengths that includes love, kindness and social intelligence
options.why: That describes humanity.

questions.explanation: Transcendence is the category of character strengths that includes gratitude, hope, humor and appreciation of beauty.

questions.stem: Seven students took a memory test. Their scores were 9, 7, 7, 1, 10, 4, 18. What is the mode of the scores?

options.why: Correct. The mode is the score that occurs most often.
That is the mean.
That is the range.
That is the highest score.

questions.explanation: In order, the scores are 1, 4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 18. The mode is the score that occurs most often. The one very high score pulls the mean (8) above the median (7), so the distribution is positively skewed.

questions.stem: Although he is not hungry, Karl buys a cake because it looks and smells delicious. Which theory of motivation best explains this?

options.why: Homeostasis is the body's tendency to keep its internal state, such as temperature, steady.
Self-determination theory is the theory that people are motivated by needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness, either from within or from outside.
Correct. Incentive theory is the theory that behavior is pulled by rewards from outside the person.
Drive-reduction theory is the theory that a physical need creates a state of tension that motivates behavior to reduce it.

questions.explanation: Incentive theory is the theory that behavior is pulled by rewards from outside the person.

questions.stem: In myasthenia gravis, receptors for one neurotransmitter are blocked, which causes muscle weakness. Which neurotransmitter is affected?

options.why: Substance P is the neurotransmitter that carries pain messages to the brain.
Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, which is involved in memory.
Norepinephrine is the neurotransmitter that helps control alertness and arousal.
Correct. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter that enables muscle movement, learning and memory.

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter that enables muscle movement, learning and memory.

questions.stem: Students who are told that another group usually does badly on a test perform slightly better than usual themselves. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: A fixed mindset is the belief that intelligence is set and cannot be changed.
An achievement test is a test that measures what a person has already learned.
Correct. Stereotype lift is the boost in performance that comes from awareness that another group is negatively stereotyped.
A growth mindset is the belief that intelligence can be developed through effort and learning.

questions.explanation: Stereotype lift is the boost in performance that comes from awareness that another group is negatively stereotyped.

questions.stem: During a near-miss in traffic, glands above the kidneys release a hormone that makes the driver's heart race. Which hormone is this?

options.why: Melatonin is the hormone released by the pineal gland that makes a person sleepy.
Correct. Adrenaline is the hormone released by the adrenal glands that raises heart rate and energy during stress.
Oxytocin is the hormone that promotes bonding, trust and social attachment.
Ghrelin is the hormone released by an empty stomach that increases hunger.

questions.explanation: Adrenaline is the hormone released by the adrenal glands that raises heart rate and energy during stress.

questions.stem: A three-year-old says that the moon is following her and that her teddy bear is sad. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Egocentrism is the difficulty that young children have in taking another person's point of view.
Object permanence is the understanding that things continue to exist when they are out of sight.
Conservation is the understanding that quantity stays the same when shape or arrangement changes.
Correct. Animism is the belief of young children that lifeless objects have feelings and intentions.

questions.explanation: Animism is the belief of young children that lifeless objects have feelings and intentions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the operational definition of the dependent variable?

options.text: The time in seconds before each participant left the room to report the smoke
options.why: Correct. An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

options.text: The random assignment of each one to a condition
options.why: This is a control procedure, not a definition of a variable.
This names the variable but does not say how it was measured.

options.text: The number of other people present
options.why: This is the independent variable.

questions.explanation: An operational definition states exactly how a variable is measured.

questions.stem: Alcohol belongs to which category of psychoactive drugs?

options.why: A hallucinogen is a drug, such as marijuana, that distorts perception and can cause sensory experiences without sensory input.
A stimulant is a drug, such as caffeine or cocaine, that speeds up neural activity and body functions.
Correct. A depressant is a drug, such as alcohol, that slows neural activity and body functions.
An opioid is a drug, such as heroin, that relieves pain by acting on endorphin receptors and is highly addictive.

questions.explanation: A depressant is a drug, such as alcohol, that slows neural activity and body functions.

questions.stem: An eight-month-old learns about a rattle by shaking it, looking at it and putting it in her mouth. Which of Piaget's stages is she in?

options.why: The preoperational stage is Piaget's stage from about age 2 to 7, in which children use words and images but cannot yet reason logically.
Correct. The sensorimotor stage is Piaget's stage from birth to about age 2, in which infants know the world through senses and actions.
The formal operational stage is Piaget's stage from about age 12 on, in which people can reason about abstract and hypothetical ideas.
The concrete operational stage is Piaget's stage from about age 7 to 11, in which children think logically about real objects and events.

questions.explanation: The sensorimotor stage is Piaget's stage from birth to about age 2, in which infants know the world through senses and actions.

questions.stem: Which stage of sleep is called paradoxical sleep because the brain is active while the body is nearly paralyzed?

options.why: Correct. REM sleep is the sleep stage with rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, an active brain and relaxed muscles.
REM rebound is the tendency to have more REM sleep after being deprived of it.
NREM stage 1 is the brief, light first stage of sleep, in which a person may have hypnagogic sensations such as falling.
The circadian rhythm is the body's roughly 24-hour cycle of wakefulness and sleep.

questions.explanation: REM sleep is the sleep stage with rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, an active brain and relaxed muscles.

questions.stem: What is the dependent variable in this study?

options.text: The facial expression produced by holding a pen
options.why: This was manipulated by the researchers: it is the independent variable.
A hypothesis is a prediction, not a variable.

options.text: The condition to which each one was assigned
options.why: This describes the independent variable.
Correct. The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome that the researchers measured.

questions.stem: A theorist argues that a gifted dancer and a gifted mathematician show different, separate kinds of intelligence. Which theory is this?

options.why: General intelligence is the single underlying mental ability that Spearman believed affects performance on all mental tasks.
The Flynn effect is the steady rise in average intelligence test scores over the generations.
Correct. Multiple intelligences is the theory that people have several independent kinds of intelligence, such as musical and interpersonal.
Mental age is the level of performance typical of a certain chronological age on an intelligence test.

questions.explanation: Multiple intelligences is the theory that people have several independent kinds of intelligence, such as musical and interpersonal.

questions.stem: Selye found that animals under prolonged stress passed through alarm, then resistance, then exhaustion. What is this three-phase pattern called?

options.why: The exhaustion phase is the third phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body's resources run out and illness becomes more likely.
The alarm reaction is the first phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the sympathetic nervous system is suddenly activated.
The resistance phase is the second phase of the general adaptation syndrome, in which the body stays highly aroused to cope with a continuing stressor.
Correct. The general adaptation syndrome is Selye's three-phase description of the body's response to long-term stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.

questions.explanation: The general adaptation syndrome is Selye's three-phase description of the body's response to long-term stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as a state of extreme energy, overconfidence, racing thoughts and little need for sleep?

options.why: Bipolar II disorder is the disorder in which a person alternates between depression and a milder form of mania called hypomania.
Major depressive disorder is the disorder in which a person has at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest, with other symptoms such as changes in sleep and appetite.
Persistent depressive disorder is the disorder in which a person has a mildly depressed mood on most days for at least two years.
Correct. Mania is a state of extreme energy, overconfidence, racing thoughts and little need for sleep.

questions.explanation: Mania is a state of extreme energy, overconfidence, racing thoughts and little need for sleep.

questions.stem: In the middle of laughing at a joke, Viktor suddenly falls asleep. Which sleep disorder does he most likely have?

options.why: Correct. Narcolepsy is a sleep disorder with sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep, often straight into REM sleep.
Insomnia is a sleep disorder with ongoing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
REM sleep behavior disorder is a sleep disorder in which the normal paralysis of REM sleep is missing, so the person acts out dreams.
Sleep apnea is a sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, causing brief awakenings.

questions.explanation: Narcolepsy is a sleep disorder with sudden, uncontrollable attacks of sleep, often straight into REM sleep.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources?

options.why: Correct. The broaden-and-build theory is the theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources.
Universal emotions is the basic emotions, such as happiness, sadness, fear and anger, whose facial expressions are recognized across cultures.
A display rule is a cultural rule about which emotions may be shown, when and to whom.
The facial-feedback hypothesis is the idea that the expression on a person's face can influence the emotion the person feels.

questions.explanation: The broaden-and-build theory is the theory that positive emotions widen a person's awareness and help build lasting skills and resources.

questions.stem: Which statement about the results is best supported?

options.text: The study shows that the two conditions always give identical results
options.why: A non-significant result does not show that there is no effect at all.

options.text: The independent variable had a large effect
options.why: The averages are close and the difference is not significant.

options.text: The difference between the groups is statistically significant
options.why: A p value of 0.41 is far above 0.05.

options.text: The difference between the groups is not statistically significant, so it could easily be due to chance
options.why: Correct. A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

questions.explanation: A p value above 0.05 means a difference this size would often occur by chance alone.

questions.stem: The gratitude group reported higher life satisfaction. The difference was statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The type of journal and subjective well-being are related, but no cause can be inferred
options.why: That limit applies to correlational studies; this was an experiment.

options.text: The same result would be found in every group of people or animals
options.why: The sample limits how far the result can be generalized.

options.text: The type of journal caused the difference in subjective well-being
options.why: Correct. With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

options.text: The hypothesis has been proved, so the study need not be repeated
options.why: Findings must be replicated; one study does not prove a hypothesis.

questions.explanation: With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

questions.stem: In the strange situation, a toddler shows little reaction when her mother leaves and turns away when she returns. Which attachment style is this?

options.why: Contact comfort is the comfort from physical touch that Harlow showed is more important to attachment than feeding.
Anxious attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child is very upset by separation and is not easily comforted on reunion.
Correct. Avoidant attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child seems indifferent when the caregiver leaves and ignores the caregiver on return.
Separation anxiety is the distress that infants show when a familiar caregiver leaves, which peaks around 13 months.

questions.explanation: Avoidant attachment is the insecure attachment style in which a child seems indifferent when the caregiver leaves and ignores the caregiver on return.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the tendency to respond to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus?

options.why: Acquisition is in classical conditioning, the first stage, in which the neutral stimulus is paired with the unconditioned stimulus and the response is learned.
Extinction is the weakening of a conditioned response when the conditioned stimulus is repeatedly presented alone.
Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of a weakened conditioned response after a rest period.
Correct. Stimulus generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus.

questions.explanation: Stimulus generalization is the tendency to respond to stimuli that are similar to the conditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: Information learned after drinking several cups of coffee is recalled best after drinking coffee again. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: A retrieval cue is a stimulus that helps bring a memory to mind.
Correct. State-dependent memory is the improved recall that occurs in the same physical state as when the information was learned.
Context-dependent memory is the improved recall that occurs in the same place where the information was learned.
Recall is the retrieval of information without any cues, as in an essay question.

questions.explanation: State-dependent memory is the improved recall that occurs in the same physical state as when the information was learned.

questions.stem: A second study of a different pair of measures finds r = −0.55. Which relationship is stronger?

options.text: Neither, because relationships with different signs cannot be compared
options.why: Strength can be compared by distance from zero.

options.text: The relationship in the first study, because its coefficient is closer to zero
options.why: A coefficient closer to zero shows a weaker relationship.

options.text: The relationship with the positive sign, whatever its size
options.why: The sign shows direction, not strength.

options.text: The relationship in the second study, because its coefficient is farther from zero
options.why: Correct. The strength of a correlation is its distance from zero, whatever the sign.

questions.explanation: The strength of a correlation is its distance from zero, whatever the sign.

questions.stem: Maya decides to raise her hand in class, and her arm muscles respond. Which part of the nervous system carries out this voluntary movement?

options.why: The autonomic nervous system is the division of the peripheral nervous system that controls glands and internal organs without conscious effort.
Correct. The somatic nervous system is the division of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles.
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
The peripheral nervous system is the sensory and motor nerves that connect the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body.

questions.explanation: The somatic nervous system is the division of the peripheral nervous system that controls voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles.

questions.stem: The group with mismatched colors named fewer flavors correctly. The difference was statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The color of the drinks and flavor identification are related, but no cause can be inferred
options.why: That limit applies to correlational studies; this was an experiment.

options.text: The hypothesis has been proved, so the study need not be repeated
options.why: Findings must be replicated; one study does not prove a hypothesis.

options.text: The same result would be found in every group of people or animals
options.why: The sample limits how far the result can be generalized.

options.text: The color of the drinks caused the difference in flavor identification
options.why: Correct. With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

questions.explanation: With random assignment and a manipulated variable, an experiment supports a conclusion about cause and effect.

questions.stem: Alex's inner sense of being a boy has been clear to him since early childhood. Which term describes this inner sense?

options.why: Gender is the socially and culturally influenced attitudes, feelings and behaviors that a culture links to being a boy, girl, man or woman.
Sexual orientation is the direction of a person's enduring sexual attraction.
Sex is the biological characteristics, such as chromosomes and anatomy, by which people are classified as male, female or intersex.
Correct. Gender identity is a person's own sense of being male, female, neither or some combination.

questions.explanation: Gender identity is a person's own sense of being male, female, neither or some combination.

questions.stem: Paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders belong to which cluster?

options.why: Cluster C is the group of personality disorders marked by anxious or fearful behavior: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive.
Cluster B is the group of personality disorders marked by dramatic, emotional or erratic behavior: antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic.
A personality disorder is a lasting, rigid pattern of behavior and inner experience that differs from cultural expectations and impairs functioning.
Correct. Cluster A is the group of personality disorders marked by odd or eccentric behavior: paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal.

questions.explanation: Cluster A is the group of personality disorders marked by odd or eccentric behavior: paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a compulsion?

options.text: A repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety
options.why: Correct. This is what a compulsion means.

options.text: The disorder in which a person has flashbacks, nightmares, watchfulness and avoidance for more than a month after a terrifying event
options.why: That describes posttraumatic stress disorder.

options.text: The disorder in which a person cannot remember important personal information, usually after trauma and with no physical cause, sometimes with travel away from home (fugue)
options.why: That describes dissociative amnesia.

options.text: The disorder in which a person has unwanted repeated thoughts and feels driven to perform repeated actions
options.why: That describes obsessive-compulsive disorder.

questions.explanation: A compulsion is a repeated action that a person feels driven to perform to reduce anxiety.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is explaining the study to participants afterward.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.
That is how subjects are placed in conditions.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: Before taking part, each participant was told what the study would involve and what the risks were, and then agreed to take part. Which ethical guideline does this meet?

options.why: Debriefing happens after the study.
Correct. Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.
Confidentiality is keeping participants' data private.
That is a research procedure, not an ethical guideline.

questions.explanation: Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.

questions.stem: Before taking part, each participant was told what the study would involve and what the risks were, and then agreed to take part. Which ethical guideline does this meet?

options.why: Confidentiality is keeping participants' data private.
Debriefing happens after the study.
That is a research procedure, not an ethical guideline.
Correct. Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.

questions.explanation: Participants must agree to take part after being told what the study involves.

questions.stem: In the early 1900s, some officials used test scores to justify laws that prevented certain people from having children. This is an example of which of the following?

options.why: A twin study is research that compares identical and fraternal twins to estimate the influence of heredity.
The evolutionary perspective is the approach that explains behavior through natural selection of traits that helped ancestors survive and reproduce.
Nature is the influence of inherited genetic factors on behavior and mental processes.
Correct. Eugenics is the discredited movement that misused ideas about heredity to argue for selective breeding of humans.

questions.explanation: Eugenics is the discredited movement that misused ideas about heredity to argue for selective breeding of humans.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the neurons inside the brain and spinal cord that pass messages between sensory inputs and motor outputs?

options.why: The reflex arc is the simple automatic pathway in which the spinal cord produces a response before the brain is aware of the stimulus.
Correct. Interneurons is the neurons inside the brain and spinal cord that pass messages between sensory inputs and motor outputs.
Glial cells is the cells that support, nourish, insulate and protect neurons.
Sensory neurons is the neurons that carry incoming information from the sense receptors to the brain and spinal cord.

questions.explanation: Interneurons is the neurons inside the brain and spinal cord that pass messages between sensory inputs and motor outputs.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the directionality problem in this study?

options.text: It is unclear whether the correlation is positive or negative
options.why: The sign of r shows the direction of the relationship.

options.text: It is unclear whether the first measure influences the second or the second influences the first
options.why: Correct. A correlation cannot show which variable, if either, comes first.

options.text: It is unclear whether the two measures were recorded
options.why: Both measures were recorded.

options.text: It is unclear how many people took part
options.why: The sample size is stated.

questions.explanation: A correlation cannot show which variable, if either, comes first.

questions.stem: After losing a match, Eli thinks, 'I always fail at everything, and it is all my fault.' Which explanatory style is this?

options.why: The self-serving bias is the tendency to credit our successes to ourselves and blame our failures on outside factors.
Relative deprivation is the feeling of being worse off than the people one compares oneself with.
The fundamental attribution error is the tendency, when judging other people's behavior, to overestimate personal traits and underestimate the situation.
Correct. A pessimistic explanatory style is the habit of explaining bad events as lasting, affecting everything and caused by oneself.

questions.explanation: A pessimistic explanatory style is the habit of explaining bad events as lasting, affecting everything and caused by oneself.

questions.stem: A sixteen-year-old tries out different friend groups, styles and beliefs to decide what kind of person she wants to be. Which of Erikson's stages is this?

options.why: Generativity versus stagnation is Erikson's stage in middle adulthood, in which people seek to contribute to the world through family and work.
Integrity versus despair is Erikson's stage in late adulthood, in which people look back on life with satisfaction or regret.
Intimacy versus isolation is Erikson's stage in young adulthood, in which people seek close, lasting relationships.
Correct. Identity versus role confusion is Erikson's stage in adolescence, in which teenagers work out who they are.

questions.explanation: Identity versus role confusion is Erikson's stage in adolescence, in which teenagers work out who they are.

questions.stem: Students are asked whether each word on a list rhymes with 'cat'. Which level of processing does this task use?

options.why: Semantic encoding is the deep encoding of a word based on its meaning.
Correct. Phonemic encoding is the encoding of a word based on its sound.
Structural encoding is the shallow encoding of a word based on its appearance.
Implicit memory is the memory of skills and learned associations that is retained without conscious recall.

questions.explanation: Phonemic encoding is the encoding of a word based on its sound.

questions.stem: Leah is sure a fact is true but cannot remember whether she read it in a textbook or saw it in a film. This best illustrates which of the following?

options.why: Correct. Source amnesia is the inability to remember where, when or how a piece of information was learned.
Imagination inflation is the increased confidence that an event happened after repeatedly imagining it.
Constructive memory is the building of a memory at retrieval from stored pieces, expectations and later information.
The misinformation effect is the distortion of a memory by misleading information received after the event.

questions.explanation: Source amnesia is the inability to remember where, when or how a piece of information was learned.

questions.stem: A baby whose cries are answered with food and comfort learns that the world is dependable. Which of Erikson's stages is this?

options.why: Autonomy versus shame and doubt is Erikson's stage in toddlerhood, in which children learn to do things for themselves.
Correct. Trust versus mistrust is Erikson's stage in infancy, in which babies learn whether their needs will be met.
Initiative versus guilt is Erikson's stage in the preschool years, in which children learn to start tasks and carry out plans.
Industry versus inferiority is Erikson's stage in elementary school, in which children learn to feel competent or else feel inadequate.

questions.explanation: Trust versus mistrust is Erikson's stage in infancy, in which babies learn whether their needs will be met.

questions.stem: To remember the order of the planets, students learn a sentence whose words start with the same letters. What is this kind of memory aid called?

options.why: Massed practice is study that is crammed into one long session.
Correct. A mnemonic device is a memory aid that uses vivid images or organizing tricks.
The method of loci is the mnemonic of imagining items placed at locations along a familiar route.
Chunking is the organizing of items into familiar, manageable units.

questions.explanation: A mnemonic device is a memory aid that uses vivid images or organizing tricks.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the mesosystem?

options.text: In ecological systems theory, the relationships between the groups in a child's immediate surroundings
options.why: Correct. This is what the mesosystem means.

options.text: In ecological systems theory, the groups that have direct contact with the child, such as family and school
options.why: That describes the microsystem.

options.text: In ecological systems theory, the life stage and historical events that affect a child
options.why: That describes the chronosystem.

options.text: In ecological systems theory, the cultural values, laws and customs that surround a child
options.why: That describes the macrosystem.

questions.explanation: The mesosystem is in ecological systems theory, the relationships between the groups in a child's immediate surroundings.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the Big Five trait of being kind, trusting and cooperative?

options.why: Conscientiousness is the Big Five trait of being organized, careful and self-disciplined.
Openness to experience is the Big Five trait of being imaginative, curious and willing to try new things.
Emotional stability is the Big Five trait of being calm and secure rather than anxious and moody.
Correct. Agreeableness is the Big Five trait of being kind, trusting and cooperative.

questions.explanation: Agreeableness is the Big Five trait of being kind, trusting and cooperative.

questions.stem: English speakers say 'white house' while Spanish speakers say 'casa blanca', with the adjective second. This difference is one of which of the following?

options.why: A phoneme is the smallest distinctive unit of sound in a language.
A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning.
Semantics is the rules by which we get meaning from words and sentences.
Correct. Syntax is the rules for ordering words into sentences.

questions.explanation: Syntax is the rules for ordering words into sentences.

questions.stem: Before releasing a new test, its makers give it to a large representative sample so that later scores can be compared with that group. What is this process called?

options.why: Test-retest reliability is the consistency of scores when the same people take the same test twice.
Split-half reliability is the consistency of scores between two halves of the same test.
Predictive validity is the extent to which test scores forecast the future performance they are meant to predict.
Correct. Standardization is the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group.

questions.explanation: Standardization is the giving and scoring of a test in the same way for everyone, and the comparison of scores with a pretested group.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do?

options.why: The self-actualizing tendency is in humanistic theory, the inborn drive of people to grow and fulfill their potential.
Correct. Unconditional positive regard is the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do.
A defense mechanism is in psychodynamic theory, a method the ego uses without awareness to reduce anxiety by distorting reality.
The unconscious is in psychodynamic theory, the store of thoughts, wishes and memories that a person is not aware of but that still influences behavior.

questions.explanation: Unconditional positive regard is the attitude of total acceptance toward another person, whatever they say or do.

questions.stem: Another research team repeats this study with new subjects and obtains the same result. What is this called?

options.why: That is how subjects are placed in conditions.
That is an in-depth study of one individual.
Correct. Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.
That is explaining the study to participants afterward.

questions.explanation: Replication is repeating a study to see whether the finding holds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the passive giving up that follows repeated experiences of being unable to avoid bad events?

options.why: Correct. Learned helplessness is the passive giving up that follows repeated experiences of being unable to avoid bad events.
Instinctive drift is the tendency of a trained animal to return to its natural, inborn behaviors.
Shaping is the reinforcing of closer and closer approximations of a desired behavior.
A primary reinforcer is a reinforcer, such as food or water, that satisfies a biological need and is rewarding without learning.

questions.explanation: Learned helplessness is the passive giving up that follows repeated experiences of being unable to avoid bad events.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a hallucination?

options.text: The jumbled, illogical speech, sometimes called word salad, that is a symptom of schizophrenia
options.why: That describes disorganized speech.

options.text: A sensory experience, such as hearing voices, that occurs without any outside stimulus
options.why: Correct. This is what a hallucination means.

options.text: A lack of emotional expression in the face and voice
options.why: That describes flat affect.

options.text: A disturbance of movement in which a person may remain motionless for hours or move without purpose
options.why: That describes catatonia.

questions.explanation: A hallucination is a sensory experience, such as hearing voices, that occurs without any outside stimulus.

questions.stem: A doctor prescribes a fast-acting drug that calms a patient's panic by slowing central nervous system activity, warning that it can cause dependence. Which kind of drug is this?

options.why: Lithium is the mood-stabilizing drug used to treat bipolar disorder.
An antipsychotic drug is a drug that reduces hallucinations and delusions by blocking dopamine receptors.
An antidepressant is a drug, such as an SSRI, that treats depression and anxiety by raising the availability of serotonin or norepinephrine.
Correct. An antianxiety drug is a drug that reduces tension by depressing central nervous system activity and can be addictive.

questions.explanation: An antianxiety drug is a drug that reduces tension by depressing central nervous system activity and can be addictive.

questions.stem: Why is this study not an experiment?

options.why: Experiments also use numerical data.

options.text: The researchers did not manipulate a variable or randomly assign anyone to conditions
options.why: Correct. An experiment requires a manipulated independent variable and random assignment.
Experiments also test hypotheses.
Sample size does not determine the research method.

questions.explanation: An experiment requires a manipulated independent variable and random assignment.

questions.stem: A researcher tests the same 200 children every two years from age 6 to age 30. Which research design is this?

options.why: Correct. A longitudinal study is research that follows the same people and retests them over a long period.
Nature and nurture is the developmental question of how heredity and experience together shape a person.
Discontinuous development is the view that development happens in distinct stages, like a staircase.
A cross-sectional study is research that compares people of different ages at one point in time.

questions.explanation: A longitudinal study is research that follows the same people and retests them over a long period.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes volley theory?

options.text: The ability to tell where a sound comes from, using differences in timing and loudness between the two ears
options.why: That describes sound localization.

options.text: Hearing loss caused by damage to the hair cells of the cochlea or to the auditory nerve
options.why: That describes sensorineural deafness.

options.text: The theory that groups of neurons take turns firing so that together they match high sound frequencies
options.why: Correct. This is what volley theory means.

options.text: Hearing loss caused by damage to the eardrum or the bones of the middle ear
options.why: That describes conduction deafness.

questions.explanation: Volley theory is the theory that groups of neurons take turns firing so that together they match high sound frequencies.

questions.stem: After the birth of a new baby, a six-year-old starts sucking his thumb and talking like a toddler. Which defense mechanism is this?

options.why: Reaction formation is the defense mechanism of acting in the opposite way to one's unacceptable impulses.
Sublimation is the defense mechanism of turning unacceptable impulses into socially valued activities.
Repression is the defense mechanism of pushing anxiety-arousing thoughts and memories out of awareness.
Correct. Regression is the defense mechanism of retreating to behavior from an earlier stage of development.

questions.explanation: Regression is the defense mechanism of retreating to behavior from an earlier stage of development.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the view that disorders involve behaviors that once helped survival but are now harmful?

options.why: The sociocultural perspective is the view that disorders result from social and cultural factors, such as poverty and discrimination.
The biological perspective is the view that disorders result from genetic, brain or chemical causes.
Correct. The evolutionary perspective is the view that disorders involve behaviors that once helped survival but are now harmful.
The humanistic perspective is the view that disorders result from blocked personal growth and a lack of acceptance.

questions.explanation: The evolutionary perspective is the view that disorders involve behaviors that once helped survival but are now harmful.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best described as the perception of motion when a series of still images or lights is shown in quick succession?

options.why: Correct. Apparent movement is the perception of motion when a series of still images or lights is shown in quick succession.
Color constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same color under different lighting.
Shape constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same shape even when the viewing angle changes.
Size constancy is the perception that an object keeps the same size even when its image on the retina changes.

questions.explanation: Apparent movement is the perception of motion when a series of still images or lights is shown in quick succession.

questions.stem: Ines cannot stand doing the same task twice and becomes restless whenever life is predictable. Which form of sensation seeking is this?

options.why: Disinhibition is the form of sensation seeking that involves a loss of self-restraint, as at wild parties.
Experience seeking is the form of sensation seeking that involves a desire for new experiences through travel, art and unusual lifestyles.
Thrill and adventure seeking is the form of sensation seeking that involves a desire for risky physical activities.
Correct. Boredom susceptibility is the form of sensation seeking that involves a strong dislike of repetition and routine.

questions.explanation: Boredom susceptibility is the form of sensation seeking that involves a strong dislike of repetition and routine.

questions.title: Article analysis: a study of aggressive behavior

parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the method as an experiment.
rubric.example: The study is an experiment: the researchers manipulated a variable and randomly assigned the subjects to conditions.

parts.prompt: State the operational definition of aggressive behavior.

rubric.criterion: States how the variable was measured in this study.
rubric.example: Aggressive behavior was defined as the number of times that each child hit the doll during ten minutes of free play.

parts.prompt: Describe the meaning of the difference between the two group averages.

rubric.criterion: Accurately describes which group scored higher or lower and what that means for the variable measured.
rubric.example: The group that watched the aggressive adult hit the doll more often. On average, the value was 14.2 for the group that watched the aggressive adult and 3.1 for the group that watched the quiet adult, and a p value of 0.01 means a difference this large is unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.prompt: Identify at least one ethical guideline applied by the researchers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies an ethical guideline that the summary shows was followed.
rubric.example: Informed consent and assent: parents consented and each child agreed to take part. (Also acceptable: approval by an institutional review board; the right to withdraw.)

parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the research findings may or may not be generalizable, using specific and relevant evidence from the study.

rubric.criterion: Explains a limit (or strength) of generalizability with reference to the sample.
rubric.example: The sample was 72 preschool children from one city, so the findings may not apply to people of other ages, cultures or backgrounds. Because the sample was not randomly selected from a wider population, it may not be representative.

parts.prompt: Explain how at least one of the research findings supports or refutes the researchers' hypothesis.

rubric.criterion: Uses a specific finding from the study as evidence.
rubric.example: The group that watched the aggressive adult hit the doll more often. (14.2 compared with 3.1).

rubric.criterion: Explains how the finding supports the hypothesis, using a psychological concept.
rubric.example: This supports the hypothesis that the behavior of an adult model affects aggressive behavior. Because subjects were randomly assigned, the difference can be attributed to the behavior of an adult model. The finding illustrates observational learning: people learn behaviors by watching and imitating models.

questions.title: Evidence-based question: Do rewards increase motivation?

parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim, based in psychological science, that responds to the question.

rubric.criterion: States a claim that answers the question and can be supported by the sources.
rubric.example: Rewards increase a behavior while they last, but they can reduce intrinsic motivation, so the behavior falls when the rewards stop.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources. (ii) Explain how the evidence supports your claim, using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP Psychology.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from one source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source A, children promised a certificate later chose to draw for 6.5 minutes, compared with 13.8 minutes for children who were not rewarded.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through intrinsic and extrinsic motivation: the reward gave the children an external reason for drawing, which weakened their desire to draw for its own sake.

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a psychological concept in the explanation.
rubric.example: The concept must be named and applied correctly, as in the model explanation.

parts.prompt: (i) Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source. (ii) Explain how this evidence supports your claim, using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding.

rubric.criterion: Uses specific, relevant evidence from a different source and names the source.
rubric.example: In Source B, workers paid a bonus made more sales (41 compared with 33), but their sales fell to 30 when the bonus ended.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
rubric.example: This supports the claim through operant conditioning: the bonus acted as positive reinforcement, which increased the behavior, and when reinforcement stopped the behavior declined (extinction).

rubric.criterion: Correctly applies a different psychological concept from the one used in part B.
rubric.example: The concept must differ from the one used in part B and be applied correctly.
